claim: In one orbit Earth travels roughly 940 million km.
pre_check: Derived: circumference of a ~150 million km radius orbit ≈ 2π × 150,000,000 ≈ 942 million km.
fact_check_evidence: In one sidereal year Earth travels about 940 million km (584 million mi) around the Sun at an average distance of about 149.6 million km. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_orbit)

claim: Calendar years have 365 days but an orbit takes about 365.25 days, so calendars add an extra day (February 29) about every four years to stay in step with the seasons.
fact_check_evidence: NASA Space Place: an orbit takes about 365.25 days, so a day is added about every four years (Feb 29) to keep the calendar in step. (https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/leap-year/en/ https://www.britannica.com/science/leap-year-calendar)

claim: As Earth orbits the Sun, the night side of Earth faces different parts of space, so different constellations are visible in different seasons.
fact_check_evidence: NASA Space Place: as Earth orbits, its night side faces different directions in space, so different constellations appear through the year. (https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/constellations/en/)

claim: Orion is a prominent evening constellation in Northern Hemisphere winter.
pre_check: Confirm the page mentions Orion as a winter constellation, or attach a better source.
fact_check_evidence: Orion is best seen in the Northern Hemisphere on winter evenings, and is high in the south around 9 to 10 p.m. in January. (https://earthsky.org/tonight/orion-the-hunter-is-easy-to-spot/ https://www.constellation-guide.com/seasonal-constellations/winter-constellations/)

claim: The International Astronomical Union officially recognizes 88 constellations.
fact_check_evidence: The IAU recognizes 88 constellations, listed in 1922 with boundaries approved in 1928 and published in 1930. (https://iauarchive.eso.org/public/themes/constellations/ https://starchild.gsfc.nasa.gov/docs/StarChild/questions/88constellations.html)

claim: Officially, each constellation is a region of the sky with set boundaries, and together they cover the whole sky.

claim: Constellations began as patterns of stars that people named after figures, animals and objects.
fact_check_evidence: NASA Space Place: constellations were named long ago after objects, animals and people seen in star patterns. (https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/constellations/en/)

claim: The stars in a constellation are usually at very different distances from Earth and only appear close together from our viewpoint.
fact_check_evidence: NASA Space Place: stars in a constellation may look close from Earth but can be very far apart; e.g., Orion's belt stars lie about 817, 1340 and 916 light-years away. claim: The Big Dipper is not an official constellation; it is an asterism, part of the constellation Ursa Major (the Great Bear).

fact_check_evidence: Polaris lies about 0.7 degree from the north celestial pole, so it appears nearly fixed while other stars circle it. (https://earthsky.org/astronomy-essentials/north-star-movement/ https://www.space.com/15567-north-star-polaris.html)

claim: Polaris is not the brightest star in the night sky; Sirius is.
fact_check_evidence: Polaris (magnitude about 2.0) ranks around 48th in brightness; Sirius (magnitude -1.46) is the brightest star in the night sky. (https://www.farmersalmanac.com/north-star-brightest-star https://www.sciencing.com/1863568/myth-north-star-isnt-brightest-star-sky/)

claim: In the Northern Hemisphere, Polaris’s height above the horizon in degrees is roughly equal to your latitude.
fact_check_evidence: In the Northern Hemisphere, Polaris's altitude above the horizon approximately equals the observer's latitude. (https://www.nsta.org/science-teacher/science-teacher-marchapril-2023/fram-polar-expedition-and-determining-latitude https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumpolar_star)

claim: The Southern Hemisphere has no bright pole star; navigators have used the Southern Cross to find south.
pre_check: Confirm; the Southern Cross is commonly used to locate the south celestial pole.
fact_check_evidence: The nearest naked-eye star to the south celestial pole, Sigma Octantis, is only magnitude 5.5 and of little use for navigation; observers use the Southern Cross to locate the pole. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigma_Octantis https://www.skyatnightmagazine.com/advice/south-star)

claim: From mid-northern latitudes, stars near Polaris circle it and never set; these are called circumpolar stars.

claim: The astronomical unit (AU) is about 150 million km, roughly the average distance between Earth and the Sun. Since 2012 it has been fixed at exactly 149,597,870.7 km.

fact_check_evidence: The AU was historically conceived as the mean Earth-Sun distance, but since 2012 the IAU defines it as exactly 149,597,870,700 m, a fixed unit roughly equal to that average distance. claim: Kepler’s laws gave the relative distances of the planets, but astronomers still needed one real distance to set the scale.
fact_check_evidence: Kepler's third law gave planetary distances in AU but not the AU's size; one absolute distance (e.g. Mars parallax 1672, transits of Venus) set the scale. (https://annex.exploratorium.edu/venus/question4.html https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/March19/Mignard/Mignard2.html)

claim: Astronomers observed the transits of Venus across the Sun in 1761 and 1769 from around the world to measure the Earth–Sun distance.

Mars orbits about 1.5 times farther from the Sun than Earth does (about 1.5 AU).
pre_check: Confirm on the Mars facts page instead if needed (~1.52 AU).
fact_check_evidence: Mars's mean distance from the Sun is about 1.52 AU (228 million km), about 1.5 times Earth's. (https://lco.global/spacebook/solar-system/mars/ https://www.skyatnightmagazine.com/space-science/how-far-is-mars-from-sun)

claim: William Herschel discovered Uranus in 1781, the first planet discovered using a telescope.
fact_check_evidence: Herschel found Uranus on 13 March 1781 with his own telescope; Science Museum and RMG describe it as the first planet discovered with a telescope. (https://www.sciencemuseum.org.uk/objects-and-stories/uranus-first-planet-discovered-telescope https://www.rmg.co.uk/stories/space-astronomy/astronomy/discovery-uranus)

claim: Before 1781, astronomers had recorded Uranus several times but mistaken it for a star.
pre_check: e.g. John Flamsteed in 1690. Confirm on the page or attach a better source.
fact_check_evidence: Uranus was recorded as a star many times before Herschel's 1781 discovery, e.g. by Flamsteed as '34 Tauri' in 1690 and by Bradley; more than 20 pre-discovery sightings are known. claim: Johann Galle spotted Neptune within about 1° of Le Verrier’s predicted position.

claim: The solar wind blows a vast bubble around the Sun and planets called the heliosphere.
fact_check_evidence: NASA: the solar wind creates a bubble around the planets called the heliosphere. (https://science.nasa.gov/heliophysics/focus-areas/heliosphere/)

claim: Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, the outer edge of the heliosphere, in 2012, entering interstellar space.
fact_check_evidence: NASA: Voyager 1 entered interstellar space on 25 August 2012 at about 122 AU; the team accepts this as the heliopause crossing date (confirmed in 2013). (https://science.nasa.gov/mission/voyager/interstellar-mission/ https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-spacecraft-embarks-on-historic-journey-into-interstellar-space/)

claim: As Earth orbits the Sun, a nearby star appears to shift slightly against more distant stars; this shift is called parallax.
fact_check_evidence: Stellar parallax is the apparent shift of a nearby star against more distant stars as Earth moves around its orbit. (https://www.britannica.com/science/stellar-parallax https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellar_parallax)

claim: The closer a star is, the larger its parallax shift, so measuring the shift gives its distance.
fact_check_evidence: Parallax is inversely proportional to distance (d in parsecs = 1/p in arcseconds), so closer stars show larger shifts. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallax_in_astronomy https://sci.esa.int/web/education/-/35616-stellar-distances)

claim: A parsec, the distance at which a star’s parallax would be one arcsecond, is about 3.26 light-years.
The European Space Agency’s Gaia spacecraft has measured the positions and distances of more than a billion stars.
fact_check_evidence: Gaia DR3 gives positions for about 1.8 billion sources and parallaxes (distances) for about 1.46 to 1.47 billion stars. (https://www.cosmos.esa.int/web/gaia/dr3 https://arxiv.org/pdf/2012.05220)

claim: How bright a star looks from Earth depends both on how much light it actually gives off (its luminosity) and on how far away it is.
A star’s apparent brightness falls with the square of its distance: twice as far away, it looks a quarter as bright.
fact_check_evidence: Apparent brightness is inversely proportional to distance squared; a source twice as far appears one quarter as bright. (https://www.astronomynotes.com/starprop/s3.htm https://courses.ems.psu.edu/astro801/content/l4_p4.html)

claim: Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, is both more luminous than the Sun and relatively close, about 8.6 light-years away.
fact_check_evidence: Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky, about 8.6 light-years away and about 25 times more luminous than the Sun. (https://www.space.com/21702-sirius-brightest-star.html https://earthsky.org/brightest-stars/sirius-the-brightest-star/)

claim: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram plots stars by their luminosity and their surface temperature.
fact_check_evidence: The H-R diagram plots stellar luminosity against surface (effective) temperature, with temperature increasing to the left. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hertzsprung%E2%80%93Russell_diagram https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/astronomy-and-astrophysics/hertzsprung-russell-diagram)

claim: The diagram is named after Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell, who developed it independently in the early 1900s.
fact_check_evidence: Hertzsprung (1911) and Russell (1913) created the diagram independently, neither knowing of the other's work, consistent with 'early 1900s'. (https://www.atnf.csiro.au/resources/education/senior-astrophysics/stellarevolution/hrintro/ https://www.britannica.com/science/Hertzsprung-Russell-diagram)

claim: Most stars, including the Sun, fall along a diagonal band on the diagram called the main sequence.
fact_check_evidence: About 90 percent of stars, including the Sun, lie on the main sequence, a diagonal band on the H-R diagram. (https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/astronomy-and-astrophysics/hertzsprung-russell-diagram https://lco.global/spacebook/stars/h-r-diagram/)

claim: The Sun sits near the middle of the main sequence: an average star in temperature and luminosity.
Red giants appear in the upper right of the diagram (cool but very luminous) and white dwarfs in the lower left (hot but dim).
fact_check_evidence: On the H-R diagram, cool but luminous giants lie at upper right and hot, dim white dwarfs at lower left. (https://www.britannica.com/science/Hertzsprung-Russell-diagram https://astro.unl.edu/naap/hr/hr_background3.html)

claim: A main-sequence star is one fusing hydrogen into helium in its core; stars spend most of their lives this way.
fact_check_evidence: Main-sequence stars fuse hydrogen into helium in their cores, and stars spend about 90% of their lives in this stage. (https://www.space.com/22437-main-sequence-star.html https://courses.lumenlearning.com/suny-astronomy/chapter/evolution-from-the-main-sequence-to-red-giants/)

claim: The observable universe is the part we can see, limited by how far light has traveled since the Big Bang; it is not the edge of the universe.
How big the whole universe is, and whether it is infinite, is unknown.
